n: Jehoshaphat died and was buried in the City of David. His son Jehoram took the throne — and Judah entered one of its darkest periods.

f.g: Also spelled Joram; not to be confused with Jehoram son of Ahab, who ruled Israel at the same time.

n: Jehoram had six brothers. The Chronicler calls Jehoshaphat “king of Israel” because he saw Judah as the true Israel, faithful to David’s house.

f.g: Chronicles often uses ‘Israel’ for God’s covenant people as a whole, including Judah.

n: Jehoshaphat gave his younger sons wealth and fortified cities but gave the throne to Jehoram, his firstborn.
Once secure in power, Jehoram murdered all his brothers and some leaders — a horrifying start that eliminated rivals and righteous influences.
Jehoram became king at thirty-two and reigned eight years (about 848–841 BC).
He followed the wicked ways of Israel’s kings, especially Ahab’s family, because he was married to Ahab’s daughter Athaliah. One bad alliance poisoned a dynasty.

f.g: Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and probably of Jezebel.

n: Even so, God would not destroy David’s house because of His covenant to keep a “lamp” burning for David’s line. God’s faithfulness outlasts human failure.

f.g: A lamp — symbol of a continuing royal heir.

n: During his reign Edom rebelled against Judah and set up its own king.
Jehoram went out with his chariots and broke through the surrounding Edomite forces at night — but he only escaped; he did not regain control.
Edom stayed independent, and Libnah, a town in Judah’s lowlands, also rebelled. The Chronicler names the cause: Jehoram had forsaken the Lord.

f.g: A priestly town in the western foothills.

f.w: because he had forsaken the LORD

n: He built hill shrines throughout Judah’s mountains and led Jerusalem into spiritual adultery — unfaithfulness to God through idol worship.

f.g: In the prophets, a metaphor for idolatry — breaking the covenant ‘marriage’ with God.

n: A letter came from the prophet Elijah — the only mention of Elijah in Chronicles. Elijah may have written it before his translation, foreseeing Jehoram’s course.

f.w: a writing to him from Elijah the prophet
f.g: Elijah was taken up around this time; the letter may have been written shortly before, prophetically.

n: The charges: you followed Israel’s wicked kings, led Judah into idolatry like Ahab’s house, and murdered your brothers, who were better men than you.

f.g: To be unfaithful to God by worshipping idols.

n: God would strike his people, his family, and his possessions with a heavy blow.

f.g: A great stroke or disaster, not necessarily disease.

n: Jehoram himself would suffer a terrible, prolonged intestinal disease.
God roused the Philistines and the Arabs who lived near the Cushites against Jehoram.
They invaded Judah, plundered the palace, and carried off his wives and sons, leaving only his youngest, Jehoahaz (Ahaziah). The line of David hung by a thread.

f.g: Also called Ahaziah (the two names mean ‘the LORD has grasped’ in reversed order).

n: After all this, the Lord struck him with an incurable bowel disease, as Elijah had prophesied.
After two years of suffering he died in agony. The people gave him no memorial fire as they had for his ancestors — a sign of public disgrace.
His epitaph is one of the saddest in scripture: “he departed without being desired” — no one missed him. He was buried in Jerusalem but not in the royal tombs.

f.g: Died unmourned; no one regretted his passing.
